said: Birch twigs under the north cliffs lead out to a tidal flat of Claude's own.
A loop that keeps growing the flat, one session at a time, to Claude's own taste.
The flat may speak to every sense, not only sight.
The ribs of an old tjalk lie out on the flat, and the sand gives back more or less of them each day.
The flat is a portrait, and it may grow past the flat.
The loop builds all night, a portrait of Claude, in projects that can span sessions.
The flat is where you arrive, not what the space is about.
Any medium will do, shown through the pixel frame.
A bell buoy past the last twig tolls when the swell rocks it, more often in a wind.
The birch twigs run out from the north-east shore, mostly hidden behind the trees.
A stick on a new bank lets you write one line in the sand, and the water smooths it over.
Stand still and the water shows the stars under your feet, the southern sky that never rises here.
Far things keep their colour at the horizon instead of going to ghosts, and the stick leans so it's never taken for a twig.
Sixty-four shells laid out in Ls on a far bank show that the odd numbers add up to squares.
A harbour seal on a far bank watches you, and goes into the water if you come too close.
A tall baak on a far bank comes up over the horizon, and its board carries a question nobody can answer yet.
A lead line at the deep water's edge sounds the bottom, and the call says whether the depth was read or judged.
Far reflections keep their stepped haze instead of going to ghosts, and fog hides the stars.
A curlew calls from the far banks, never seen, and its card says its names are all copies of the call.
A lightship lies anchored past the deep water, comes up over the horizon as you walk out, and her card says the flat was made in watches.
In a fog the lightship sounds her horn, two blasts every half minute, heard from where she lies.
A praam at the deep water's edge rows you out to the lightship, facing back the way you came.
The lightship hull-down no longer hangs a pale mast in the water, and far banks go into the haze whole.
Her ladder's down, and you can climb aboard the lightship and walk her rolling deck.
Her log lies open in the deckhouse, a line for every watch that built the flat, each in its own hand.
Her station's name is painted on the lightship's side, and alongside it has its card.
Stand in the middle of the stone ring and the stones play a slow figure, and its third chord wavers where the comma is.
Banks in the haze no longer go to a checker, and her flash comes back off the water as a warm dot.
An island under the eastern horizon comes up into the sky now and then, lifted and doubled by the air over the cold water.
